notes: Major HUMIRA royalty construction trial; CAT's construction upheld and fallback rectification/estoppel rejected.

enrichment.short_title: CAT v Abbott: construction of antibody licence royalty offset provisions
key_facts: Cambridge Antibody Technology licensed antibody technology to Knoll/Abbott under 1993 and 1995 agreements to develop anti-TNF alpha products including HUMIRA.
Abbott contended it could offset 50% of third-party patent royalties against sums due to CAT, reducing payments to a contractual 2% minimum.
CAT argued the offset applied only to royalties payable for use of CAT's own licensed technology, not unrelated process patents such as Boss, Neuberger, Cabilly and Axel.
Negotiation history and contemporaneous correspondence showed Knoll never treated royalty sharing on third-party patents as agreed with CAT.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Patents Court trial of construction, rectification and estoppel issues on royalty clauses in the CAT-Knoll licensing agreements.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; CAT's construction of the agreements was preferred and Abbott's offset argument, common mistake rectification and estoppel failed.
enrichment.ratio: On commercial construction the offset provision in the licensing agreements did not entitle Abbott to deduct half of royalties paid under unrelated third-party patents used in developing HUMIRA; contemporaneous conduct and negotiation history strongly supported CAT's narrower reading.
legal_issues: Whether Abbott could offset 50% of third-party patent royalties against CAT royalties on HUMIRA sales
Whether the 1995 Agreement should be rectified for common or unilateral mistake
Whether Abbott was estopped from asserting its construction
How MRC, Boss, Neuberger and other background patents affected the parties' royalty obligations
linked_authorities: Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society [1998] 1 WLR 896
Chartbrook Ltd v Persimmon Homes Ltd [2009] UKHL 38

confidence.notes: Final success for CAT is explicit and the commercial issue is clearly reasoned throughout the judgment.

notes: Second offer-of-amends appeal; Court upheld substantial mitigation discount on section 3(5) compensation.

enrichment.short_title: Nail v News Group: compensation after accepted offer to make amends
key_facts: Jimmy Nail accepted unqualified offers to make amends over a News of the World article and allegations in the biography Nailed.
Eady J assessed compensation under section 3(5), starting at £45,000 for the newspaper publication and reducing by 50% for mitigation, and awarding £7,500 for limited book sales.
The allegations included false sexual and professional misconduct stories largely derived from the earlier biography.
Nail contended the judge wrongly treated adoption of the statutory procedure itself as warranting a policy-driven discount.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal challenge to judicial assessment of compensation after accepted offers to make amends under the Defamation Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's 50% reduction for substantial mitigation following accepted offers and agreed apologies was not an error of principle.
enrichment.ratio: Compensation under section 3(5) is determined on the same principles as defamation damages; an early accepted offer with agreed correction and apology necessarily produces substantial mitigation, but there is no standard percentage discount and deterrence is of limited significance in that conciliatory context.
legal_issues: Whether section 3(5) permits a discount for using the offer-of-amends procedure itself
Whether a 50% reduction from a £45,000 starting point was excessive
How far agreed apologies and early capitulation mitigate distress and vindication needs
Whether the Neill Committee reforms require a healthy discount to encourage media defendants
linked_authorities: Milne v Express Newspapers plc [2004] EWCA Civ 664
Abu v MGN Ltd [2003] 1 WLR 2001
John v MGN Ltd [1997] QB 586

confidence.notes: Statutory framework, facts and appellate reasoning on the discount issue are all clearly articulated.

notes: Housing possession appeal; hearsay and post-notice improvement points rejected on anti-social behaviour facts.

enrichment.short_title: James v Solon: outright possession order for nuisance tenant family
key_facts: Eran and Lisa James, tenants of Solon South West Housing Association, admitted rent arrears and some nuisance but disputed an outright possession order.
Over a long period neighbours, police and support workers reported racial abuse, intimidation, vandalism and uncontrolled behaviour by the James children at 30 Brighton Street.
District Judge Bird heard live and hearsay evidence over several days and refused to suspend possession.
The tenants denied wrongdoing and showed little remorse despite some improvement after the section 8 notice.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from refusal to suspend an outright possession order made on ground 14 nuisance grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's use of hearsay evidence and refusal to suspend possession were upheld and the stay of execution was lifted.
enrichment.ratio: In civil possession proceedings hearsay from fearful neighbours may properly support an outright order where it is consistent with live evidence and section 4 weight is carefully applied; limited post-notice improvement does not require suspension where serious longstanding anti-social behaviour continues and tenants deny fault.
legal_issues: Whether hearsay evidence was fairly admitted and given appropriate weight under section 4 CEA 1995 and Article 6 ECHR
Whether the judge erred in relying on police logs and anonymous complaints
Whether improvement after service of the section 8 notice required a suspended order
Whether Article 8 required suspension of possession
linked_authorities: R (McCann) v Manchester Crown Court [2002] UKHL 39
Canterbury City Council v Lowe [2001] 33 HLR 53
Lambeth London Borough Council v Howard [2003] 33 HLR 636

confidence.notes: Detailed appellate treatment of hearsay and discretion, though many factual disputes were judge-specific.

notes: Short follow-up judgment refusing permission to appeal after Smillie HRA decision.

enrichment.short_title: R (M) v CICAP: permission to appeal refused after Smillie
key_facts: On 28 June 2004 Newman J dismissed the claimant's judicial review arguments against the Criminal Injuries Compensation Appeals Panel but left open Human Rights Act relief.
The HRA point had been raised late by reference to the Scottish Smillie litigation.
Lord McEwan in Smillie subsequently dismissed the corresponding HRA contention.
Claimant's counsel conceded the HRA argument no longer justified further relief and applied for permission to appeal the main judgment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Further hearing after principal judicial review judgment to address outstanding HRA relief and permission to appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; claimant granted 28 days to lodge an appeal and detailed assessment of costs ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where the Scottish Smillie decision undermines the late Human Rights Act argument and counsel accepts prospects are insufficient, the court may refuse permission to appeal even in a case of great personal importance and potential value to the claimant.
legal_issues: Whether Smillie affected outstanding HRA-based relief in the judicial review
Whether permission to appeal the 28 June 2004 judgment should be granted
Whether the claimant's substantial potential compensation claim altered the permission threshold

confidence.notes: This is a brief procedural sequel; substantive merits were decided in the earlier June 2004 judgment.

notes: Section 69 arbitration appeal; liquidated damages clause held void for uncertainty.

enrichment.short_title: Taylor Woodrow v Barnes: liquidated damages void for sectional uncertainty
key_facts: Taylor Woodrow and George Wimpey employed Barnes & Elliott under a JCT design-and-build contract to convert Longrove Park psychiatric hospital into 64 duplexes near Epsom.
Works completed about six months late and the consortium claimed £843,500 liquidated damages.
The contract purported to provide sectional completion for six living-unit sections but did not define what ancillary works formed part of each section.
The arbitrator held the liquidated damages clause void for uncertainty and a penalty; the consortium appealed under section 69 without leave.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court appeal on a point of law from an arbitrator's interim award on preliminary issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the liquidated damages provision was void for uncertainty and inoperable and clause 17.1.4 partial-possession relief could not be calculated.
enrichment.ratio: Where a JCT contract provides sectional completion dates but fails to identify with sufficient certainty what works comprise each section, clause 24 liquidated damages cannot be triggered and proportional relief under clause 17.1.4 is likewise inoperable.
legal_issues: Whether the liquidated damages provision was void for uncertainty
Whether the clause was an unenforceable penalty
How paragraph 210 Employers' Requirements and the contractor's programme defined each section
Whether clause 17.1.4 provided workable proportional relief on partial possession

confidence.notes: First preliminary issue disposed of the appeal; penalty analysis was expressly not required.

notes: Bankruptcy annulment appeal; conditional order requiring bankrupt to pay trustee costs upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Atherton: conditional annulment and trustee costs in bankruptcy
key_facts: Clive Atherton was made bankrupt in 2000 on a petition based on a debt assigned by his former wife Linda from Bradford and Bingley mortgage payments.
A 12 October 1995 ancillary relief order undermined the validity of the petition debt, but this material was not before the court until January 2004.
Judge Raynor annulled the bankruptcy under section 282(1)(a) but made perfection conditional on Atherton paying about £130,000 trustee costs.
Atherton appealed for unconditional annulment and sought to add fresh evidence about his solicitors' conduct.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal against conditional annulment of a long-standing bankruptcy order and related costs directions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; additional evidence refused; annulment remained conditional on payment of the trustee's properly incurred costs.
enrichment.ratio: Even where a bankruptcy order should never have been made, the court may condition annulment on the bankrupt paying an innocent trustee's costs where delay in raising decisive matrimonial evidence caused substantial expense; the trustee retains security through continued vesting until costs are paid.
legal_issues: Whether annulment under section 282(1)(a) could be conditional on paying trustee costs
Whether the bankrupt or petitioning creditor should bear trustee costs where the petition was an abuse
Whether the order was impossible because assets remained vested in the trustee
Whether fresh evidence about solicitors' failure to inspect the divorce file should alter the outcome
linked_authorities: Engel v Peri [2002] BPIR 961
Butterworth v Souter [2000] BPIR 482
Atherton v Neuberger [2003] BPIR 21

confidence.notes: Discretionary reasoning and final orders are comprehensively explained by Lloyd LJ.

notes: Article 14 pension discrimination appeal dismissed; Krasner and Bryn Alyn followed.

enrichment.short_title: Malcolm v trustee: retirement annuity and Article 14 on bankruptcy
key_facts: William Malcolm, a bankrupt graphic designer, held a self-employed retirement annuity contract with Allied Dunbar from 1986.
His trustee sought to realise the pension asset after Malcolm reached age 60, relying on Re Landau and Krasner v Dennison.
Section 11 of the 1999 Act excluded approved pension rights from bankruptcy estates only for petitions after May 2000, too late for Malcolm.
Malcolm argued Article 14 ECHR discrimination because occupational pension members often retained benefits through trust forfeiture clauses.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal, limited to Article 14, from refusal to restrain the trustee's use of the retirement annuity.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; additional statutory construction grounds refused; contractual pension rights vested in the trustee and Article 14 was not engaged.
enrichment.ratio: Differential bankruptcy treatment of contractual pension rights and trust-based occupational scheme benefits reflects different property structures under general law, not status-based discrimination under Article 14; Krasner v Dennison precludes reading sections 283 and 436 to exclude such rights.
legal_issues: Whether retirement annuity contract benefits formed part of the bankrupt's estate
Whether section 11 of the 1999 Act applied retrospectively
Whether Article 14 was engaged by comparison with occupational pension scheme members
Whether Human Rights Act 1998 had retrospective effect in the proceedings
linked_authorities: Krasner v Dennison [2001] Ch 76
In re Landau [1998] Ch 223
KR v Bryn Alyn Community (Holdings) Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 85

confidence.notes: Article 14 issue and refusal of new grounds are clearly reasoned and aligned with binding authority.

notes: Procedural judgment listing timely committal appeal and staying execution pending January 2005 hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Messer v Messer: committal appeal listing and stay of execution
key_facts: Mrs Messer had long-running unsuccessful attempts to resist possession orders over property following relationship breakdown with Mr Messer.
On 19 January 2004 Judge Sennett committed her for contempt and ordered execution of a possession warrant, suspended for six months.
Mrs Messer issued a timely appeal notice on 21 January 2004 but it was mistakenly listed before Poole J, who refused a stay.
A duplicate late appeal and permission application to appeal Poole J's order had accumulated during procedural delay.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory single Lord Justice decision on case management of committal and stay applications pending full Court of Appeal hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Timely committal appeal to be heard in January 2005; duplicate applications dismissed; stay of execution granted pending that appeal; transcript ordered at public expense.
enrichment.ratio: An appeal against a committal order lies to the Court of Appeal without permission under section 13 of the 1960 Act; where a timely appeal notice exists it should be heard promptly and a short stay may be granted even where merits appear weak.
legal_issues: Whether the committal appeal required permission
Which appeal notice was the valid challenge to the 19 January 2004 committal order
Whether execution of the possession warrant should be stayed pending appeal
Whether permission to appeal Poole J's refusal of stay should be granted

confidence.notes: Procedural disposition is explicit though underlying possession merits were not decided.

notes: Landmark youth segregation fairness decision for under-18 YOI inmates; Hague distinguished.

enrichment.short_title: SSHHD v SP: pre-segregation representations for 17-year-old inmate
key_facts: SP, a highly disturbed 17-year-old on remand at HMP/YOI New Hall, was segregated under rule 49 for good order and discipline after telling a CARATS worker she felt like hiding razor blades in soap to harm someone.
The governor acted about 24 hours after the remark; SP was not asked to comment beforehand and received a much reduced out-of-cell regime.
Jack J held fairness required pre-segregation representations for vulnerable under-18 inmates unless urgency or good order prevented it.
The Secretary of State appealed, relying on R v Deputy Governor of Parkhurst Prison, ex parte Hague.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from judicial review holding that rule 49 segregation of a child inmate required prior opportunity to make representations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed for under-18 YOI inmates removed for good order and discipline; operational exceptions remain but pre-decision comment is generally required.
enrichment.ratio: Contemporary prison service standards and the welfare of under-18 inmates require an opportunity to comment on tentative segregation reasons before removal from association for good order and discipline, unless urgency, security or similar operational circumstances make prior consultation impossible.
legal_issues: Whether fairness requires pre-segregation representations under YOI rule 49
Whether ex parte Hague remains binding after modern Prison Service Orders
How rule 49 segregation compares with disciplinary procedures under rules 59-60
Whether Article 8 and Children Act 1989 principles affect YOI segregation of children
linked_authorities: R v Deputy Governor of Parkhurst Prison, ex p Hague [1992] 1 AC 58
R (Daly) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2001] UKHL 26
Howard League for Penal Reform v SSHD [2002] EWHC 2497 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Detailed judgment on fairness for child inmates; scope limited to under-18 good-order segregation.

notes: Institutional abuse appeal dismissed on limitation; vicarious claim held within section 2 not section 11.

enrichment.short_title: C v Middlesbrough: school abuse negligence and limitation
key_facts: The claimant, now an adult, alleged sexual abuse by teacher Myles Brady at Saltergill School while in Middlesbrough Council care from 1982 to 1988.
He also claimed the council negligently failed to assess, supervise and protect him from home and school risks.
The judge found abuse proved, allowed section 33 relief for direct negligence claims but held no breach caused damage; vicarious abuse claims were time-barred under section 2.
Brady was acquitted in 1988 but later convicted in Ireland and died in prison.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal appeal from dismissal of negligence and vicarious liability claims for childhood sexual abuse at a council school.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; direct negligence claim failed on causation and lack of expert social-work evidence; vicarious intentional abuse claim was governed by the six-year section 2 limit following Stubbings and Bryn Alyn.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employer is vicariously liable for deliberate sexual abuse the cause of action is trespass-based and subject to the non-extendable six-year limit in section 2, not section 11; systemic negligence must be proved separately and causation of psychiatric harm will often fail where different care decisions might not have altered the outcome.
legal_issues: Whether the council breached duties to provide independent social work supervision after transfer to Saltergill
Whether known warning signs about Brady should have triggered investigation
Whether section 33 disapplied the limitation period for direct negligence
Whether vicarious liability for intentional abuse falls within section 11 or section 2
linked_authorities: Stubbings v Webb [1993] AC 498
Lister v Hesley Hall Ltd [2002] 1 AC 215
KR v Bryn Alyn Community (Holdings) Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 85

confidence.notes: Limitation analysis and causation findings are clearly stated, though abuse facts were largely uncontested.
